questions.prompt: A max-heap is represented in a zero-based array. For a node at index i, its parent index is
questions.explanation: In a zero-based heap array, the parent of a nonroot node i is floor((i-1)/2).

questions.prompt: In a zero-based binary heap array, what is the right child index of node 6?
questions.explanation: The right child index is 2i+2, so for i=6 it is 14.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, which relation holds between every parent and its children?
options: Parent key is at least each child key
Parent key is at most each child key
Keys increase from left to right at every level
Every node is greater than every node in the next level
answer: Parent key is at least each child key
questions.explanation: The max-heap property constrains each parent to be no smaller than its children; it does not sort nodes within a level or across subtrees.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the array representation of a binary heap is true?
options: It is a complete binary tree
It is always a full binary tree
Every leaf has the same depth
answer: It is a complete binary tree
questions.explanation: A binary heap is structurally complete, with the final level filled from left to right, enabling compact array storage.

questions.prompt: A binary heap contains 31 elements. What is the index of its last element in a zero-based array?
questions.explanation: With n elements, occupied indices are 0 through n-1; the last index for 31 elements is 30.

questions.prompt: The maximum element in a max-heap is found in
questions.explanation: Every parent is at least its descendants by repeated heap inequalities, so the global maximum is at the root.

questions.prompt: Inserting an element into a binary heap with n elements takes worst-case time
questions.explanation: The new element is placed at the next complete-tree position and may bubble up at most the heap height, which is O(log n).

questions.prompt: A complete binary heap has 63 nodes. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: A perfect tree of height 5 has 2^6-1=63 nodes, so the heap height is 5.

questions.prompt: During max-heap insertion, the new key is repeatedly swapped with its parent while
questions.explanation: To restore max-heap order, a newly inserted key moves upward while it exceeds its parent; the process stops when the parent is at least as large or root is reached.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has height 4. What is the maximum number of swaps needed to bubble up one inserted key?
questions.explanation: An insertion starts at a leaf at depth at most four and can swap once per edge on the path to the root.

questions.prompt: Removing the maximum element from a max-heap takes
questions.explanation: After removing the root, the last element is moved to the root and sifted downward at most the heap height, which is logarithmic.

questions.prompt: After deleting the root of a max-heap, which element is moved to the root before heap restoration?
options: The last element in level-order array storage
answer: The last element in level-order array storage
questions.explanation: Removing the final array element preserves completeness. Moving it to the root leaves one position to restore with sift-down.

questions.prompt: A max-heap root has children 14 and 18. During sift-down, which child should it be compared/swapped with first?
questions.explanation: To preserve the max-heap order, sift-down swaps with the larger child, which is 18.

questions.prompt: Which operations on a binary max-heap have O(log n) worst-case time?
options: Increase the key of a known node
answer: Increase the key of a known node
questions.explanation: Insertion, extract-max, and increase-key can follow a path of heap height. Finding an arbitrary key has no ordering shortcut and may scan all n elements.

questions.prompt: Building a heap by inserting n keys one at a time has worst-case time
questions.explanation: Each insertion may take O(log n), so n successive insertions have O(n log n) worst-case total time.

questions.prompt: Bottom-up build-heap on an array of n keys runs in
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near leaves and sift down only a few levels. Summing node-height costs across all levels yields linear total time.

questions.prompt: Bottom-up build-heap on an array of 15 elements starts heapifying at what zero-based index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)-1. For n=15 this is floor(15/2)-1=6.

questions.prompt: In bottom-up heap construction, which nodes need sift-down processing?
options: Internal nodes, in reverse level order
Nodes from the root downward in preorder
answer: Internal nodes, in reverse level order
questions.explanation: Leaves already satisfy heap order. Processing internal nodes bottom-up ensures child subtrees are heaps before each parent is sifted down.

questions.prompt: Which statements about bottom-up heap construction are true?
options: It can be faster asymptotically than n successive insertions
It starts with leaves as trivial heaps
Its worst-case time is Theta(n log n)
answer: It can be faster asymptotically than n successive insertions
It starts with leaves as trivial heaps
questions.explanation: Leaves are already heaps; internal nodes are processed bottom-up. The sum of potential sift-down distances is linear, whereas successive insertion has O(n log n) bound.

questions.prompt: A max-heap stores distinct values. If its root is 100, what can be concluded about the second-largest value?
options: It is one of the root's children
It is the last array element
answer: It is one of the root's children
questions.explanation: Any node other than the root is below one of its children in the heap tree, and the largest nonroot key must be one of the root's immediate children.

questions.prompt: A min-heap supports extract-min in
questions.explanation: The minimum is at the root. Replacing it with the final element and sifting down takes at most the heap height, O(log n).

questions.prompt: In a min-heap, the key at the root is
options: no greater than any other key
no smaller than any other key
answer: no greater than any other key
questions.explanation: The min-heap property ensures every parent is no greater than its children, so the root is a global minimum.

questions.prompt: A complete binary min-heap has 127 elements. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: Since 127=2^7-1, it is perfect with levels 0 through 6, so height is 6.

questions.prompt: Which array index range contains leaves of a zero-based heap with n elements?
questions.explanation: An index i is a leaf when its left child 2i+1 is outside the occupied range. This begins at floor(n/2).

questions.prompt: A zero-based heap has 20 elements. What is the last internal-node index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)-1=floor(20/2)-1=9.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a binary heap are true?
options: Its array supports O(1) access to the root
A search for an arbitrary key is O(log n) worst case
answer: Its array supports O(1) access to the root
questions.explanation: Completeness allows compact array storage and provides the root at index zero. Heap order does not sort the array, and arbitrary-key search may be linear.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [50,30,40,10,20,35]. Is it a valid max-heap?
options: Yes, every parent is at least its children
No, the array must be sorted
answer: Yes, every parent is at least its children
questions.explanation: The root 50 exceeds children 30 and 40; node 30 exceeds 10 and 20; node 40 exceeds 35. All parent-child constraints hold.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [40,25,35,10,30,20]. Which change is required to make it a valid max-heap?
questions.explanation: At index 1, parent 25 is smaller than child 30 at index 4, violating heap order. Swapping these values fixes that relation without breaking the others.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [3,7,5,12,9,8]. What is the minimum number of parent-child violations?
questions.explanation: The root 3 is below 7 and 5; 7 is below 12 and 9; 5 is below 8. No parent-child relation violates min-heap order.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, a key at index i is increased. Which repair is generally needed?
options: Swap it with the root unconditionally
questions.explanation: Increasing a key can make it larger than its parent, so the violation is along the parent path and is repaired by sift-up.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, a key at a known index is decreased. Which repair is generally needed?
options: Move it to the final index
questions.explanation: Decreasing a key may make it smaller than one or both children. Sifting down restores parent dominance along a downward path.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has height 5. A key is decreased at the root. What is the maximum number of downward swaps required?
questions.explanation: A root-to-leaf path contains at most five edges, so sift-down performs at most five swaps.

questions.prompt: Which key updates in a max-heap may violate heap order in the upward direction?
options: Increase a key at a known node
Decrease a key at a known node
Replace a key by a larger value
Replace a key by a smaller value
answer: Increase a key at a known node
Replace a key by a larger value
questions.explanation: Increasing a key or replacing it by a larger value may exceed its parent and require sift-up. Decreasing a key can instead violate order with children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap is not a search tree because
options: siblings and subtrees are not ordered by key ranges
it is stored in an array
answer: siblings and subtrees are not ordered by key ranges
questions.explanation: Heap order compares each parent only with its children; it does not require all keys in one subtree to be ordered relative to another subtree.

questions.prompt: The k-th largest element can be found by repeated extract-max from a max-heap in
options: O(n+k log n) including heap construction
answer: O(n+k log n) including heap construction
questions.explanation: Build the heap in O(n), then perform k extractions at O(log n) each, for O(n+k log n).

questions.prompt: A max-heap contains 100 elements. After extracting the maximum 4 times, how many elements remain?
questions.explanation: Each extraction removes exactly one element, leaving 100-4=96.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by a binary heap provides which typical operation bounds?
options: Insert and extract-priority in O(log n), peek in O(1)
Search and delete arbitrary key in O(log n) without extra indexing
Build-heap in O(n log n) only
answer: Insert and extract-priority in O(log n), peek in O(1)
questions.explanation: Heap insertion and extraction traverse a height path; the root provides constant-time peek. Arbitrary search is not logarithmic without additional indexing.

questions.prompt: In heapsort using a max-heap, after swapping the root with the last unsorted element, the heap size is
questions.explanation: The maximum is placed at the end of the array, which is excluded from the active heap. The remaining heap shrinks by one and is restored with sift-down.

questions.prompt: Which properties hold for heapsort on an array using an in-place binary heap?
options: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
It is stable in its standard form
answer: Worst-case time is O(n log n)
questions.explanation: Heapsort runs in O(n log n) worst-case time, sorts in-place with O(1) auxiliary space, and is not stable in its standard form.

questions.prompt: Heapsort with a max-heap produces the sorted array in
questions.explanation: Repeatedly moving the maximum to the final unsorted position places values from largest to smallest at the array's right end, yielding ascending order overall.

questions.prompt: A d-ary heap is a complete tree in which each internal node can have at most
questions.explanation: The branching factor d specifies the maximum number of children per node. A binary heap is the special case d=2.

questions.prompt: In a d-ary heap, increasing d generally
options: reduces height but increases the number of children inspected during sift-down
answer: reduces height but increases the number of children inspected during sift-down
questions.explanation: Larger branching factors reduce the number of levels for n nodes, but choosing the best child during sift-down requires inspecting up to d children.

questions.prompt: A perfect 4-ary tree has height 2 measured in edges. How many nodes does it contain?
questions.explanation: A full 4-ary tree through depth 2 has 1+4+16=21 nodes.

questions.prompt: A binary min-heap is used to implement a priority queue. Which element is removed by extract-min?
questions.explanation: The root stores the minimum by heap order. Extract-min removes it, then repairs the heap after moving the final element to root.

questions.prompt: A binary min-heap stores 12 elements. How many elements are removed after 5 successful extract-min operations?
questions.explanation: Each extract-min removes one item, so five successful operations remove five elements.

questions.prompt: Which operations on a binary heap have O(1) worst-case time?
options: Read the heap size when maintained
Return the array element at a given index
answer: Read the heap size when maintained
Return the array element at a given index
questions.explanation: The root, a maintained size counter, and an array element at a supplied index can be read directly in constant time. Searching for an arbitrary key may require scanning the heap.

questions.prompt: A max-heap's root is removed and the heap has n>1 elements. Why is sift-down necessary after moving the last element to root?
options: The moved element may be smaller than a child
The tree may cease to be complete
The root must always be the most recently inserted key
answer: The moved element may be smaller than a child
questions.explanation: The last element may not dominate its children, violating max-heap order at the root. The complete shape is preserved because the final slot is removed.

questions.prompt: A min-heap contains distinct values. What is the second-smallest element guaranteed to be?
questions.explanation: The minimum is at root; the second-smallest must be the minimum among its children because any deeper node has an ancestor child no greater than it.

questions.prompt: A min-heap root has children 4 and 9, and all other nodes are descendants of these children. What is the second-smallest key?
questions.explanation: The minimum is the root. The least remaining value must be among root's children, and min(4,9)=4.

questions.prompt: A heap's array representation allows parent and child positions to be computed in
questions.explanation: Index arithmetic computes parent and child locations directly without traversing pointers, requiring constant time.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [2,5,3,9,7,8]. Which operation can return a value in O(1) time?
questions.explanation: The minimum is at the root, array index zero. The maximum and median are not generally known from heap order without additional work.

questions.prompt: A max-heap has 16 elements. How many leaves does its complete binary tree contain?
questions.explanation: In a zero-based heap, leaves occupy indices floor(n/2) through n-1. For n=16, there are 8 leaves.

questions.prompt: Which statements about a complete binary tree with n nodes stored in a heap array are correct?
options: All occupied indices form a prefix starting at zero
The final level, if partial, is filled left to right
Every node has exactly two children
answer: All occupied indices form a prefix starting at zero
The final level, if partial, is filled left to right
questions.explanation: The array occupies a prefix and the final tree level is left-packed. A complete binary tree has logarithmic height floor(log2 n); nodes can have fewer than two children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap with n elements has height
questions.explanation: The last occupied level is depth floor(log2 n), since a complete tree has 2^h through 2^(h+1)-1 nodes at height h.

questions.prompt: A complete binary heap has 100 elements. What is its height in edges?
questions.explanation: Since 2^6=64<=100<128=2^7, the height is floor(log2 100)=6.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, after a new key is appended at the end, which direction can restore heap order?
questions.explanation: The new key is a leaf, so it cannot violate order with its children. Only its relationship to ancestors can be invalid, repaired by sift-up.

questions.prompt: In a min-heap, after replacing the root with the last element, which direction is used to restore heap order?
questions.explanation: The root's children may be smaller than the replacement, while there is no parent above root. Sift-down addresses the possible violation.

questions.prompt: A binary heap has height 7. What is the maximum number of comparisons of children during one sift-down, assuming one comparison selects the better child at each level?
questions.explanation: At most one child-selection comparison is made at each of the seven levels traversed, giving seven such comparisons (excluding parent comparison).

questions.prompt: A heap is built from an array using repeated insertions. If each insertion costs O(log n), what is the resulting upper bound for n insertions?
questions.explanation: Summing n logarithmic upper bounds gives O(n log n). Bottom-up build-heap improves this to O(n), but that is a different construction method.

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of a binary heap for priority-queue implementation?
options: O(1) access to the top-priority item
O(log n) search for any arbitrary key
answer: O(1) access to the top-priority item
questions.explanation: A heap uses compact array storage, provides constant-time access to the top priority, and supports logarithmic insert/extract. Arbitrary-key search is not logarithmic in general.

questions.prompt: A max-heap stores priorities 90,70,80,20,50,60,75 in level order. What is the array after extracting the maximum and restoring heap order?
questions.explanation: Move last key 75 to root and remove 90. Compare 75 with children 70 and 80, swap with 80; the resulting heap is [80,70,75,20,50,60].

questions.prompt: A min-heap array is [4,8,6,12,10,9]. After inserting 3, what is the resulting heap array?
questions.explanation: Append 3 at index 6, swap with parent 6 at index 2, then swap with root 4. This yields [3,8,4,12,10,9,6].

questions.prompt: A max-heap array is [40,25,35,10,20,30]. After inserting 50 and bubbling up, what is the root value?
questions.explanation: 50 swaps with parent 35 at index 2, then with root 40, so the root becomes 50.

questions.prompt: A heap insertion of a value performs swaps along a root-to-leaf path. What is the maximum path length for n elements?
questions.explanation: A complete binary tree has logarithmic height, so a bubble-up path contains at most O(log n) edges.

questions.prompt: Which statements about extracting from a max-heap are true?
options: The final array element is moved to the root
The active heap size decreases by one
Sift-down may swap with the smaller child
answer: The final array element is moved to the root
The active heap size decreases by one
questions.explanation: The root is maximum, the final element replaces it, and the active size decreases by one. Sift-down in a max-heap chooses the larger child, not the smaller.

questions.prompt: When sifting down in a max-heap, if a node is smaller than both children, it should be swapped with
questions.explanation: Swapping with the larger child ensures the promoted value remains at least as large as the other child, maintaining heap order at that level.

questions.prompt: A max-heap node has children 12 and 17, and its key is 9. Which value becomes the parent after one sift-down swap?
questions.explanation: The larger child 17 is promoted to the parent's position during max-heap sift-down.

questions.prompt: A min-heap's sift-down operation chooses the smaller child because
options: the promoted child must be no greater than its sibling
the larger child is always a leaf
the root must be the largest
answer: the promoted child must be no greater than its sibling
questions.explanation: Promoting the smaller child keeps it no greater than the sibling, which is necessary for both children to remain at least the new parent in a min-heap.

questions.prompt: A min-heap node has children 6 and 11 and key 15. Which child is selected for a sift-down swap?
questions.explanation: For min-heap restoration, choose the smaller child, 6, so the parent remains no greater than both children.

questions.prompt: A binary heap permits finding an arbitrary value by scanning its array. What is the worst-case time?
questions.explanation: Heap order does not locate a target by key range; the key may be at any index, so a worst-case scan checks all n elements.

questions.prompt: A max-priority queue stores tasks by priority in a max-heap. If equal priorities are allowed, does heap order guarantee FIFO among tied tasks?
options: No, additional sequence information or tie-breaking is needed
Only when the heap has odd size
answer: No, additional sequence information or tie-breaking is needed
questions.explanation: Heap order constrains priority values but not the relative order of equal-priority items. Stable tie handling requires explicit arrival-order data and comparison rules.

questions.prompt: Which information can be included in heap keys to provide deterministic tie-breaking?
options: Current array index only, if indices change after swaps
questions.explanation: Priority is the primary field; a sequence number can preserve FIFO among ties, and a unique identifier can complete deterministic comparison. Array index changes during swaps, so it is not stable tie information.

questions.prompt: A stable priority queue can compare pairs (priority, sequence). For equal priority, which sequence order preserves FIFO?
options: Compare the task payload alphabetically only
questions.explanation: Assigning increasing sequence numbers at insertion and favoring the smaller number among equal priorities preserves arrival order.

questions.prompt: A heap has 10 items and uses a one-based array with index 1 as root. What is the left-child index of node 6?
questions.explanation: With one-based heap indexing, the left child index is 2i=12.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap array has a node at index i. Its right child is at index
questions.explanation: One-based indexing gives left child 2i and right child 2i+1.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap stores n elements at indices 1 through n. Which index range contains leaves?
questions.explanation: Indices greater than floor(n/2) have left-child indices beyond n, so they are leaves.

questions.prompt: A one-based heap has 17 elements. What is the last internal-node index?
questions.explanation: The last internal node is floor(n/2)=floor(17/2)=8.

questions.prompt: The bottom-up heapify process can start at index floor(n/2)-1 because
options: the root is always a leaf
all earlier indices are already heaps
the array is sorted from the midpoint onward
questions.explanation: In zero-based storage, nodes from floor(n/2) onward have no children. They are trivial heaps, so processing begins at the last internal node.

questions.prompt: Which facts explain why bottom-up heap construction is linear?
options: There are about n/2 leaves with zero sift-down distance
Only about n/4 nodes can move down one level
Only about n/8 nodes can move down two levels
Every node moves down log n levels
answer: There are about n/2 leaves with zero sift-down distance
Only about n/4 nodes can move down one level
Only about n/8 nodes can move down two levels
questions.explanation: About n/2 leaves have zero height; fewer nodes can descend one or more levels as distance grows. The geometric weighted sum is O(n), unlike moving every node log n levels.

questions.prompt: The root of a max-heap is 100. What is the minimum possible key among all other nodes?
options: It may be arbitrarily smaller subject to the key domain
It must be one of the root's children
answer: It may be arbitrarily smaller subject to the key domain
questions.explanation: Heap order imposes an upper-bound relation from parent to child, but a descendant can have a very small value; there is no global lower bound from the root.

questions.prompt: A min-heap is used for Dijkstra's algorithm with adjacency lists and decrease-key support. What is the heap operation required when a shorter distance to a vertex is found?
questions.explanation: A shorter tentative distance decreases that vertex's priority key in a min-priority queue, requiring decrease-key and upward repair.

questions.prompt: A binary heap priority queue without a direct handle to a vertex uses lazy insertion in Dijkstra's algorithm. How is a stale extracted entry recognized?
options: Compare its stored distance with the current best distance
Check whether it is the last array element
Compare it with the heap root's parent
answer: Compare its stored distance with the current best distance
questions.explanation: When an old pair is extracted, if its distance exceeds the current best recorded distance for that vertex, it is stale and can be skipped.

questions.prompt: A shortest-path implementation inserts 3 tentative distance entries for the same vertex into a heap. If the best known distance is 12 and an extracted entry has distance 17, what is the distance gap indicating staleness?
questions.explanation: The extracted value exceeds the current best by 17-12=5, so it is stale.

questions.prompt: Which statements about using a binary heap in Prim's minimum spanning tree algorithm are correct?
options: The heap can store candidate vertices keyed by best incident edge weight
Extract-min chooses a next vertex with minimum current key
A key decrease may be needed when a cheaper connecting edge is found
The heap itself guarantees the resulting graph is connected
answer: The heap can store candidate vertices keyed by best incident edge weight
Extract-min chooses a next vertex with minimum current key
A key decrease may be needed when a cheaper connecting edge is found
questions.explanation: The heap stores each candidate vertex keyed by its best connecting edge; extract-min selects the cheapest candidate, and decrease-key updates improved edges. Connectivity depends on the graph, not the heap.

questions.prompt: For a binary heap with n entries, decrease-key on a known node handle takes
questions.explanation: A decreased key in a min-heap bubbles upward along a root path whose length is O(log n).

questions.prompt: A min-heap node at depth 3 has its key decreased enough to reach the root. What is the maximum number of swaps?
questions.explanation: A node at depth three has three edges to the root, so at most three upward swaps are needed.

questions.prompt: A binary heap is complete, but does that imply its array is sorted?
options: No, only parent-child heap order is required
Only if the heap has an even size
answer: No, only parent-child heap order is required
questions.explanation: Completeness describes shape; heap order is local. Siblings and cousins are not necessarily sorted relative to each other.

questions.prompt: A max-heap array [90,70,80,20,60,75,65] is valid because
options: each parent is at least its children
answer: each parent is at least its children
questions.explanation: Root 90 exceeds 70 and 80; 70 exceeds 20 and 60; 80 exceeds 75 and 65. These parent-child checks establish a valid max-heap.

questions.prompt: A min-heap array [2,6,4,9,8,7,5] has how many parent-child violations?
questions.explanation: Each parent is no greater than its children: 2<=6,4; 6<=9,8; and 4<=7,5. Thus there are no violations.

questions.prompt: In heapsort, the heap is built from an arbitrary array and then repeatedly reduced. What is the total worst-case running time?
questions.explanation: Bottom-up build is O(n), followed by n extract-max operations costing O(log n) each. The total is Theta(n log n).

questions.prompt: Which structures can implement a priority queue with different operation trade-offs?
questions.explanation: Unsorted arrays/lists, sorted arrays/lists, and binary heaps all support priority queues with different insertion and extraction costs.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by an unsorted array supports insert in
questions.explanation: Appending an item to an unsorted array takes constant time, while extraction of an extreme priority generally requires a linear scan.

questions.prompt: A priority queue implemented by a sorted array supports find-min in
options: O(1) if the minimum is kept at an endpoint
answer: O(1) if the minimum is kept at an endpoint
questions.explanation: If the array is maintained in sorted order, the minimum lies at a known endpoint and is accessible in constant time; insertion may require shifting O(n) items.

questions.prompt: An unsorted array priority queue contains 40 elements. In the worst case, how many key comparisons are needed to extract the maximum?
questions.explanation: A linear scan can initialize the candidate from one element and compare the other 39 elements against it.

questions.prompt: A binary heap's height is logarithmic because it is
questions.explanation: Completeness ensures every level except the last is full and the last is left-packed, giving logarithmic height in the number of nodes.

questions.prompt: A max-heap supports delete-key for an arbitrary node in O(log n) when
options: a handle to its array index is available
answer: a handle to its array index is available
questions.explanation: With a handle, replace the target by the last element, remove the last slot, and sift up or down as needed, taking heap-height time.

questions.prompt: A heap has height 8. An arbitrary key replacement may require either sift-up or sift-down. What is the maximum number of swaps along one repair path?
questions.explanation: The repair follows at most one root-to-leaf path, whose length is bounded by heap height eight.

questions.prompt: After replacing a heap element at index i by a new key, which repair direction is needed in a max-heap?
options: Up if it exceeds its parent; otherwise down if below a child
Both up and down in separate full traversals
answer: Up if it exceeds its parent; otherwise down if below a child
questions.explanation: Only one side of the local ordering can be violated based on the new key relative to its parent and children; the corresponding path is repaired.

questions.prompt: Which comparisons identify whether a changed key in a max-heap requires sift-up or sift-down?
options: Compare it with its parent when i is not root
If it is smaller than a child, sift-down may be needed
If it is greater than its parent, sift-up may be needed
Compare it with every heap element
answer: Compare it with its parent when i is not root
If it is smaller than a child, sift-down may be needed
If it is greater than its parent, sift-up may be needed
questions.explanation: The parent comparison detects whether a larger value violates upward order; child comparisons detect a smaller value that may violate downward order. A full scan is unnecessary for a known index.

questions.prompt: A min-heap stores all distinct values 1 through 15. Which value is guaranteed at the root?
questions.explanation: The root of a min-heap is the global minimum, which among these distinct keys is 1.
